overview.text: RNA, or ribonucleic acid, is a nucleic acid that helps cells use and regulate genetic information. It is made by copying DNA in transcription and is often—but not always—single-stranded; its four bases are adenine, uracil, cytosine, and guanine. RNA is not just a temporary message: messenger RNA (mRNA) carries protein-making instructions to ribosomes, transfer RNA (tRNA) delivers amino acids, and ribosomal RNA (rRNA) helps form ribosomes and catalyze protein assembly. Other RNAs regulate gene activity; for example, small interfering RNAs can guide the breakdown of matching mRNA, reducing protein production. This variety makes RNA central to gene expression and control.

key_facts.text: RNA is often single-stranded, but some RNA molecules are not; RNA contains the bases A, U, C, and G.
Ribosomes read mRNA in three-nucleotide units called codons to help assemble proteins.
tRNA folds into a distinctive L-shape; one end matches an mRNA codon, while another carries an amino acid.
In RNA interference, small interfering RNA (siRNA) guides a complex to matching mRNA, which can then be cleaved and degraded.
Other gene-regulating RNAs include microRNAs, which can block protein production, and long noncoding RNAs, which have varied regulatory roles.
